title: 1.1.3b Why Documentation Matters
description: One paragraph on why documentation matters in real software work, with a specific example. AI-graded with hints.

aiGrader.prompt:
In one paragraph (about 100–150 words), explain why documentation matters in professional software development.

Documentation means comments in the code and notes like a README that explain what the code does and how to use it.

Your paragraph must include one specific example. You can use any of these:
- A messy program you had to read and the comments (or missing comments) you wished it had.
- Your own A3.1 refactor, where you added comments and a README to a messy program.
- A hypothetical: imagine a teammate (or future-you, six months later) opening this code with no documentation — what goes wrong, and how does documentation prevent it?

Write in your own words. A generic 'documentation is good because it helps' with no concrete example will not be enough.

rubric.title: Clear explanation of why documentation matters
rubric.description: Student gives a real reason documentation matters in professional work — e.g., other people (or future-you) have to read and maintain the code, onboarding new teammates, remembering intent months later, reducing bugs from misunderstanding. Full credit for a clear, correct reason in their own words. Deny if the answer is empty, off-topic, or only restates 'documentation is important' with no reasoning.

rubric.title: One specific, non-generic example
rubric.description: Student includes a concrete example — their A3.1 refactor, a specific messy-code experience, or a fleshed-out hypothetical with an actual scenario (who reads the code, what breaks without docs). Full credit requires specificity. Deny for vague hand-waving like 'for example it helps people' with no actual situation described.

rubric.title: Clear writing, roughly one paragraph
rubric.description: The response is a coherent paragraph in roughly the 100–150 word range and is easy to read. Deny this criterion only for significant issues: a single sentence, far over/under length, or writing too disorganized to follow.
